name: Pattern Noise Mapping
description: Maps fixed pattern noise (FPN) and dark current patterns unique to camera sensors — absent in AI-generated content (Healey & Kondepudy, 1994).
mechanism:
This method extracts and analyzes fixed pattern noise (FPN) embedded in camera images to identify the source sensor and detect AI-generated content:

1. **Noise Residual Extraction**: The sensor noise residual W is extracted by subtracting a denoised version of the image from the original: W = I − F(I), where F is a denoising filter (typically BM3D or wavelet-based). This residual contains both random shot noise and the sensor's fixed pattern noise. The FPN component is deterministic — identical for every image captured by the same sensor — while shot noise varies randomly.

2. **Photo-Response Non-Uniformity (PRNU) Estimation**: Following Lukáš, Fridrich & Goljan (2006), the PRNU fingerprint K is estimated by averaging noise residuals from multiple images taken with the same camera: K̂ = (Σᵢ Wᵢ·Iᵢ) / (Σᵢ Iᵢ²). The PRNU represents pixel-level sensitivity variations caused by manufacturing imperfections in the silicon wafer. Each sensor has a unique PRNU pattern, functioning as an optical fingerprint with millions of independent elements.

3. **Dark Current Pattern Analysis**: In addition to PRNU, the method analyzes the dark current fixed pattern noise (DCFPN) — the signal produced by the sensor with no light exposure. DCFPN is extracted from dark regions of the image where photon shot noise is minimal. Each pixel has a characteristic dark current level that increases with temperature and exposure time. The DCFPN pattern is used to verify sensor identity in long-exposure or high-ISO images where PRNU analysis is less reliable.

4. **Forgery and AI Detection**: For a test image, the noise residual W_test is extracted and correlated with the reference PRNU K̂. The normalized cross-correlation ρ = corr(W_test, K̂·I_test) is computed. Authentic images from the reference camera produce ρ >> 0 (typically ρ > 0.01 with peak > 60 in the PCE test). AI-generated images produce ρ ≈ 0 because they lack sensor-specific PRNU patterns. For tampered images, spatial blocks with low ρ indicate manipulated regions.
parameters:
Denoising filter: BM3D (σ estimated per-image)
PRNU estimation: minimum 50 reference images
Correlation metric: Peak-to-Correlation Energy (PCE)
Authentication threshold: PCE > 60
Block size for tampering localization: 128×128 pixels
DCFPN estimation: dark frame averaging (10+ frames)
Minimum image size: 256×256 pixels
accuracy: 99.7% camera identification accuracy with PCE test (Lukáš et al., 2006). Tampering localization via blockwise PRNU: F1-score of 0.90 at 128×128 block resolution. AI-generated image detection: 97% (AI images consistently fail PRNU correlation). False positive rate < 0.1% at PCE threshold of 60.
source: Lukáš, J., Fridrich, J. & Goljan, M. (2006). Digital Camera Identification from Sensor Pattern Noise. IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security, 1(2), 205–214.
useCase: Identifying the specific camera that captured a photograph. Detecting AI-generated images that lack physical sensor noise patterns. Localizing manipulated regions within an otherwise authentic photograph. Linking multiple photos to the same camera device in forensic investigations.
strengths:
• PRNU is unique per sensor — the most reliable camera identification technique available
• AI-generated images categorically lack sensor noise patterns
• PCE-based authentication has extremely low false positive rate (< 0.1%)
• Block-wise analysis localizes tampered regions
• Works even after moderate JPEG compression and resizing
limitations:
• Requires reference images from the same camera for PRNU estimation
• Image resizing, cropping, or rotation requires geometric synchronization
• Heavy denoising or aggressive image processing reduces PRNU signal strength
• Flat-field or saturated images provide weak PRNU correlation
• Counter-forensic PRNU removal/forgery attacks exist (Gloe et al., 2007)
